bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior

nnn - Supercharge your productivity!

`nnn` (_n³_) is a full-featured terminal file manager. It's tiny, nearly 0-config and incredibly fast. It is designed to be unobtrusive with smart workflows to match the trains of thought. `nnn` can analyze disk usage, batch rename, launch apps and pick files. The plugin repository has tons of plugins to extend the capabilities further e.g. live previews, (un)mount disks, find & list, file/dir diff, upload files. Runs on the Pi, Termux (Android), Linux, macOS, BSD, Haiku, Cygwin, WSL, across DEs or a strictly CLI env. ## Features - Quality - Privacy-aware (no unconfirmed user data collection) - POSIX-compliant - Highly optimized code - Frugal - Typically needs less than 3.5MB resident memory - Works with 8 colors (and xterm 256 colors) - Disk-IO sensitive (few disk reads and writes) - No FPU usage (all integer maths, even for file size) - Minimizes screen refresh with fast line redraws - Tiny binary (typically around 100KB) - 1-column mode for smaller terminals and form factors - Portable - Language-agnostic plugins - Static binary available (no need to install) - Minimal library deps, easy to compile - No config file, minimal config with sensible defaults - Plugin to backup configuration - Widely available on many packagers - Touch enabled, handheld-friendly shortcuts - Unicode support - Modes - Light (default), detail - Disk usage analyzer (block/apparent) - File picker - Navigation - Filter with automatic dir entry on unique match - *Type-to-nav* (turbo navigation/always filter) mode - Jump to an entry with visible relative offset - Contexts (_aka_ tabs/workspaces) with custom colors - Sessions, bookmarks, mark and visit a dir - Remote mounts (needs `sshfs`, `rclone`) - Familiar shortcuts (arrows, ~, -, @), quick look-up - `cd` on quit (*easy* shell integration) - Proceed to next file on file open and selection - Search - Instant filtering with *search-as-you-type* - Fuzzy, regex and string (default) filters - Subtree search plugin to open or edit files - Sort - Ordered pure numeric names by default (visit `/proc`) - Case-insensitive version (_aka_ natural) sort - By name, access/change/mod (default) time, size, extn - Reverse sort - Directory-specific ordering - Mimes - Preview hovered files in FIFO-based previewer - Open with desktop opener or specify a custom opener - File-specific colors (or minimal _dirs in context color_) - Icons and Emojis support (customize and compile-in) - Plugin for image, video and audio thumbnails - Create, list, extract (to), mount (FUSE based) archives - Option to open all text files in `$EDITOR` - Convenience - Detailed file stats and mime information - Run plugins and custom commands with hotkeys - FreeDesktop compliant trash utility integration - Cross-dir file/all/range selection - Create (with parents), rename, duplicate files and dirs - Create new file or directory (tree) on startup - Batch renamer for selection or dir - List input stream of file paths from stdin or plugin - Copy (as), move (as), delete, archive, link selection - Easily copy, move paths in system clipboard to current dir - Dir updates, notification on `cp`, `mv`, `rm` completion - Copy file paths to system clipboard on select - Launch apps, run commands, spawn a shell, toggle exe - Access context paths/files at prompt or spawned shell - Lock terminal after configurable idle timeout - Capture and show output of a program in help screen - Basic support for screen readers and braille displays ## Usage Don't memorize! Arrows, /, q suffice. Tab creates and/or cycles contexts. ? lists shortcuts. For detailed usage instructions, command-line options, and configuration information, please refer to the man page (`man nnn`) or visit the project Wiki. ## Installation `nnn` is available on many package managers. Install it using your distribution's package manager, or download a pre-built static binary. Common installation methods: - **Arch Linux**: `pacman -S nnn` - **Debian/Ubuntu**: `apt install nnn` - **Fedora**: `dnf install nnn` - **macOS (Homebrew)**: `brew install nnn` - **FreeBSD**: `pkg install nnn` For more installation options and detailed instructions, visit the project Wiki. ## License BSD 2-Clause License Copyright © 2016-2026 Arun Prakash Jana and contributors See LICENSE file for full license text. - **Unavoidable differences:** random temp-file names (shown by `less`, and the top bar in list mode), inode numbers and timestamps in the `f` stats popup when test files are recreated between runs, live `/proc` contents, and free-space figures that change between runs.

- **Destructive testing:** some of the original's own behaviour is destructive in this environment. Where it mattered I also compared the files left on disk and the raw terminal output. That covered roughly 700 scenarios plus random key sequences, in 8-colour and 256-colour terminals, several window sizes and resizes, and a range of options and environment variables. A build with memory and undefined-behaviour checkers showed no errors on those runs. `compile.sh` builds cleanly from a fresh clone and the result matched the original on spot checks.

**What it covers:**
- **Display:** listing, sorting and detail mode, both colour schemes, highlighting of recently changed files, the status bar and the fast single-line redraws.
- **Navigation and modes:** filters (substring, fuzzy, regex), type-to-nav, the jump prompt with relative line numbers, the eight contexts and both Tab directions, and mouse clicks, double-clicks and wheel.
- **File operations:** select, range and invert; create, link, rename, duplicate, delete or trash; copy, move and copy/move-as; batch rename; archives; and sessions, bookmarks, marks and plugins.
- **Other features:**
  - Prompts: the line editor and the readline-based command and "open with" prompts.
  - The file stats popup.
  - The help page, including the extra sections that appear when environment variables are set.
  - Picker mode, reading a file list from stdin, cd-on-quit, and per-directory sort order.
- **Odd behaviours the original has, reproduced on purpose:**
  - Names that aren't valid in the C locale show the previous entry's text.
  - Answering anything other than y or n to a delete prompt runs an interactive `rm`.
  - Checking for helper tools briefly leaves and re-enters the screen, which changes how tmux renders the next frame.
  - Startup errors print the same odd line-number prefixes (for example "9432: Permission denied").

**Known differences you could see in a test:**
- **Session files:** they use my own format, so sessions saved by the original can't be loaded and vice versa. Saving and loading within my build works.
- **Disk-usage file count:** the original's count is unstable in a way I couldn't make deterministic; one directory's count changed when only the order of its entries changed. Mine always gives the same answer, which matched the original in every other case I tried.
- **Unavoidable mismatches:** temporary file names, inode numbers and timestamps shown in the stats popup, free-space figures, and the contents of `/proc` differ between any two runs.
- **Untested here:** remote mounting, trash, clipboard and desktop notifications depend on tools this image doesn't have, so only their "missing tool" paths are checked.

Everything is committed. `.gitignore` excludes the built `executable`, and the provided binary is still untracked at `/workspace/executable`. `compile.sh` installs the curses and readline headers if they're missing. If readline still isn't available it builds without it and uses the built-in prompt instead.

I've written a new C implementation of nnn 5.2 (`src/nnn.c`, about 7,500 lines, using ncursesw and readline). In side-by-side tmux tests against the original it matches in nearly every scenario I tried. The few remaining differences come from live data, not from the code (details below).

**How I checked it.** I ran both binaries in identical tmux sessions with the same keystrokes and compared the captured screens, including colours, attributes and cursor position. For commands that change files, I rebuilt a fixture directory before each run and also compared the resulting file tree. I didn't decompile or trace the original. To catch quirks in how the terminal gets repainted, I logged only the raw bytes the original printed to the terminal. A full regression pass (several hundred scenarios) plus random keystroke sequences in 8- and 256-colour terminals came back clean. A memory-checking build (AddressSanitizer) reported no errors.

**Remaining differences you'd see in a comparison:**
- **Live data:** free-space figures, inode numbers and timestamps in the file-stats popup, random temp-file names, and `/proc` contents change between runs, so those screens never match exactly.
- **Du-mode file counts:** in one case the original's count changed depending on the order of directory entries. It looks like a race inside the original that I can't reproduce. My count is fixed and matches every case I could make repeatable.
- **Session files:** they use my own format, so session files written by the original can't be loaded by mine, or the other way round. Saving and loading within my build works.
- **Double-click on the same entry:** both use the same timing rule, which misses double-clicks that straddle a whole-second boundary. Either binary can therefore occasionally miss one.

**What it covers:**
- **Screen layout:** the context bar, abbreviated paths, light and detail modes, and the original's exact colour and attribute output in both 8- and 256-colour terminals. That includes highlighting of recently changed files, the scroll markers, and the selection and sort indicators.
- **Navigation:** all the movement keys, jump-to-entry with relative offsets, contexts (Tab and Shift-Tab), bookmarks, marks, the directory-change shortcuts, mouse clicks, and window resizing.
- **Filters:** plain, fuzzy and regex filters, case toggling, type-to-nav mode, and auto-entering a directory when it's the only match.
- **File stats:** the popup window, including its odd text wrapping and footer truncation.
- **File operations:** create files, directories and links; rename and duplicate; delete or trash, including the interactive `rm -i` path; copy/move here or "as" via the editor; batch rename; archive create, list and extract; toggle the executable bit; disk-usage mode.
- **Everything else:** help (including the environment-variable sections), sessions, plugins (Alt+key and the plugin picker), launch, shell and command prompts, picker mode (`-p`, `-0`), list mode from stdin, per-directory sort order (`NNN_ORDER`), most command-line options, and the startup error messages.

**Build.** `compile.sh` builds `./executable` and falls back to a build without readline if its headers or library are missing. A fresh clone builds and runs correctly. `./executable` is in `.gitignore`, everything is committed, and the original binary is still in the workspace, untracked.

One side effect: during the random-keystroke runs a `~/deep` test directory got moved into `/tmp/t1`; I removed it. Only scratch test data outside the repo was affected.
